segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Agrippa said to Paul,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You are permitted to speak for yourself.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Paul stretched out his hand and began his defense:

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I consider myself blessed, King Agrippa, that it is before you I am about to make my defense today concerning everything I am accused of by Jews,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: especially because you are well acquainted with all the customs and disputes among Jews. So I beg you to listen to me patiently.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Now, my way of life from my youth, lived from the beginning among my own nation and in Jerusalem, is known to all Jews.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: They have known me for a long time, if they are willing to testify, that I lived as a Pharisee, according to the strictest party of our religion.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: And now I stand here on trial because of hope in the promise God made to our fathers,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: a promise our twelve tribes hope to attain as they worship earnestly night and day. It is about this hope, O king, that I am accused by Jews!

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Why is it judged unbelievable among you that God raises the dead?

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: I myself, indeed, was convinced that I ought to do many things against the name of Jesus of Nazareth.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: And that is what I did in Jerusalem. I locked up many of the holy ones in prisons, having received authority from the chief priests, and when they were being put to death I cast my vote against them.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: In all the synagogues I often punished them and tried to force them to blaspheme, and, utterly out of my mind with rage against them, I persecuted them even as far as foreign cities.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: While doing this, I was traveling to Damascus with the authority and commission of the chief priests,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: when at midday on the road, O king, I saw a light from heaven, brighter than the sun, shining around me and those traveling with me.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: We all fell to the ground, and I heard a voice saying to me in the Hebrew language,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goads.’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: And I said, ‘Who are you, Lord?’ And the Lord said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: ‘I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But get up and stand on your feet. For I have appeared to you for this purpose: to appoint you as a servant and witness both of the things in which you have seen me and of those in which I will appear to you,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: rescuing you from the people and from the Gentiles, to whom I am sending you

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: to open their eyes, so that they may turn from darkness to light and from the authority of Satan to God, and so receive forgiveness of sins and a share among those who have been made holy by faith in me.’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: So then, King Agrippa, I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: but I declared first to those in Damascus and in Jerusalem, and throughout the whole region of Judea, and to the Gentiles, that they should turn back and turn to God, doing deeds worthy of that turning back.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Because of this, Jews seized me in the temple and tried to kill me.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: So, having obtained help from God, I stand to this day testifying to both small and great, saying nothing beyond what the prophets and Moses said was going to happen:

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: that the Messiah was to suffer and that, as the first to rise from the dead, he was to proclaim light both to the people and to the Gentiles.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As he was making this defense, Festus said in a loud voice,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You are out of your mind, Paul! Your great learning is driving you out of your mind.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Paul said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I am not out of my mind, most excellent Festus, but I am declaring words of truth and of a sound mind.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: For the king knows about these things, and to him I am speaking freely. For I am not persuaded that any of this has escaped his notice, since this was not done in a corner.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Do you believe the prophets, King Agrippa? I know that you believe.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Agrippa said to Paul,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “In so little time you are trying to persuade me to become a Christian?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And Paul said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Whether in little time or much, I would pray to God that not only you but also all who are listening to me today might become such as I am—apart from these chains.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the king rose, and the governor and Bernice and those who were sitting with them,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and after withdrawing they talked with one another, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “This man is doing nothing that deserves death or chains.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And Agrippa said to Festus,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “This man could have been released if he had not appealed to Caesar.”

notes.note: The Greek word here is the same one rendered “Gentiles” in verses 17, 20 and 23. In the singular it means a people or nation, here Paul’s own; in the plural it regularly means the non-Jewish peoples. In those later verses it is set against “the people,” a standing term for Israel.

The traditional rendering is “sect,” which most translations keep. In the period the word named a recognized school or party within a larger body, as it does for the Pharisees and Sadducees, without the modern suggestion of a breakaway fringe group. “Party” is used to avoid that suggestion.

The traditional rendering is “saints,” which many translations keep. The word is used of all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing Septuagint language for Israel. “Saints” now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue.

The Greek is literally “I cast down a pebble,” the ordinary idiom for voting, since pebbles were used as ballots. If meant literally, it implies Paul sat on a body that passed sentence, perhaps the council in Jerusalem. Many scholars take it as a figure of speech for his approval of the executions; the question is unsettled.

notes.phrase: tried to force them to blaspheme
notes.note: The Greek tense can describe either a repeated action or an attempted one. Most modern translations take it as an attempt (“tried to force”), which leaves open whether Paul succeeded; older versions have “compelled,” implying that he did. To blaspheme here would mean to curse or renounce Jesus.

The phrase can mean Hebrew proper or Aramaic, the related everyday language of Jews in Judea and Galilee; Greek writers of the period did not always distinguish them. Many scholars and several translations take it as Aramaic here, but the matter is disputed. The name is given in its Semitic form, “Saoul,” not the Greek form used elsewhere in the narrative.

A goad was a pointed stick used to drive oxen; an animal that kicked back at it only hurt itself. The expression was a well-known Greek proverb for futile resistance to a greater power, especially a divine one, and is found in classical writers such as Euripides.

The verb usually means “rescue” or “deliver,” and most translations take it so here. It can also mean “choose out” or “select,” which would give “choosing you out from the people and from the Gentiles.” The first fits the verb’s other uses in Acts and the echo of God’s promise to rescue the prophet Jeremiah.

notes.phrase: those who have been made holy
notes.note: Most mainstream translations use “sanctified.” The Greek verb is built directly on the ordinary word for “holy,” the same word behind “holy ones” in verse 10, and “made holy” keeps that link visible. The closing phrase “by faith in me” may attach to being made holy or to receiving forgiveness and a share; the Greek word order allows either.

Most translations have “repent” and “repentance” here, as established terms understood to include a change of life. “Repent” now centers on feeling sorry, while the Greek word carries the prophets’ call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct. It stands here beside a second verb, “turn to God,” which names the goal of the turning.

The traditional rendering is “Christ.” Here the word is a title under discussion, the anointed king Israel expected, and not a name, so “Messiah” is used, as in several modern translations. The two clauses are introduced in Greek by “whether,” as though listing the points under debate: whether the Messiah is to suffer, and whether he is the first to rise.

notes.traditional: Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian
notes.note: Agrippa’s reply is one of the most disputed sentences in Acts. The older rendering “almost” is now generally rejected; the phrase means “in a little,” either “in a short time” or “with so little argument.” The tone may be ironic or evasive rather than sincere, and the last words can also be read as “to play the Christian.” Paul’s answer picks up the same phrase: “whether in little or in much.”

candidates.reason: Used in Acts of Pharisees, Sadducees and the Jesus movement and in the letters for factions; “sect,” “party,” “school” and “faction” all appear in translations, and the choice colors how readers see these groups.
With Ἑβραϊστί in John, Acts and Revelation, translators split between “Hebrew” and “Aramaic”; one policy is needed across books.
Occurs across the Gospels and Acts alongside Ναζαρηνός; translations vary between “of Nazareth,” “the Nazarene” and “the Nazorean,” and Acts 24:5 uses the plural of a group.
Recurs throughout the New Testament with translators alternating between “authority,” “power,” “right” and “dominion,” which obscures links such as verses 10, 12 and 18 here.
Frequently a near-technical term for Israel as God’s people over against the Gentiles; whether to render it “the people,” “your own people” or “Israel” should be decided once.
